messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel R., a 50-year-old European American psychologist, came to treatment describing a quiet but relentless change in himself after a rape that had occurred in his early adult years and that he had never fully been able to speak about. The assault had taken place after an evening when alcohol was present and he had already felt uneasy in the room; the smell of it now seemed to carry him back to the bodily panic of that night in a way he could not control. He would catch a whiff of liquor in a restaurant, or pass someone who had been drinking, and feel himself recoil internally, not only with fear but with a harsh, immediate conclusion that he was somehow diminished by what had happened. In those moments he found himself thinking, with painful certainty, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him as a clinician and a husband, and that something in him had been reduced to an object rather than a person. Even the sound of sirens could unsettle him in the same way; when they wailed down the street or outside his office, he would feel that same deadened, stripped quality settle over him, as if danger had already entered the room and confirmed his sense that he was not fully human anymore.

Over time, those appraisals had begun to shape the way Daniel related to the memory itself. He found himself pushing the event away before he could fully recall it, stopping short whenever an image or body sensation started to form, because he was afraid of being overwhelmed by the same deadness and humiliation. He could not seem to put the frightening event into words, even after years of being trained to help others do exactly that; when he tried, the story dissolved into fragments, and sometimes what came back was not an image at all but the full emotional intensity of terror and shame without a clear narrative to contain it. That wordless surge made him more convinced that the assault had taken something essential from him, and that if he allowed himself to remember in any detail he would be forced to face how completely he had been changed. He began to monitor himself closely for signs of those states, bracing whenever he felt even slightly uncomfortable in a room, because discomfort itself now seemed like the start of collapse.

As these reactions accumulated, Daniel’s daily life narrowed around the things most likely to unsettle him. In his consulting office he became wary of clients who arrived smelling of alcohol from lunch or a late afternoon happy hour nearby, and he sometimes arranged the room so he would not have to sit directly across from them when the odor was present. At home, a siren from the street could make him go silent at dinner, withdrawing into a flat, faraway watchfulness that his wife had begun to notice. He was embarrassed by how quickly his mind turned these moments into evidence that he was permanently damaged, and that belief made him more determined to avoid anything that might stir the event into mind. Yet the more he pushed the memory aside, the less he seemed able to access it at all except as a surge of dread and shame; and the less he could put into words, the more he experienced himself as dead inside, a capable professional in name only, someone who had been hollowed out and made into something to be handled rather than known. That sense of being an object, not a person, seemed to sharpen every encounter with alcohol smell, every passing siren, every flicker of unease.

By the time he sought help, the strain had begun to affect both his work and his marriage. He had started avoiding social situations where alcohol might be present and had become increasingly guarded in his clinic, fearful that a sudden smell or sound would leave him visibly shaken in front of a client. What finally brought him in was not a single dramatic crisis but the mounting fear that he was losing the parts of himself that had once mattered most, while becoming more and more unreachable to the people closest to him. Daniel wanted to know whether he could speak about the assault without shutting down, and whether the deadness he felt was permanent or could be undone, though what frightened him most was the possibility that he would remain trapped in this state of being unable to remember, unable to speak, and unable to feel like a person again.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers leading to fear and bodily panic, but it does not clearly state that the triggers cause Daniel’s negative appraisals or distorted beliefs in the same paragraph.
